entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen14824" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Judgment upon the Idolatrous Places, and on the Idol-Worshippers</title> <div sID="gen14825" type="x-p"/> To God’s address in <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.5-Ezek.5.17">Eze 5:5-17</reference>, explaining the signs in <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.1-Ezek.4.5">Eze 4:1-5</reference>, are appended in <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.1-Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:1-14</reference> and 7 two additional oracles, which present a further development of the contents of these signs, the judgment portrayed by them in its extent and greatness. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.1-Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:1-14</reference> there is announced, in the first section, to the idolatrous places, and on their account to the land, desolation, and to the idolaters, destruction (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.3-Ezek.6.7">Eze 6:3-7</reference>); and to this is added the prospect of a remnant of the people, who are dispersed among the heathen, coming to be converted to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.8-Ezek.6.10">Eze 6:8-10</reference>). In the second section the necessity and terrible character of the impending judgment is repeatedly described at length as an appendix to <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.12">Eze 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:14</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.11-Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:11-14</reference>). <div eID="gen14825" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Desolation of the Land, and Destruction of the Idolaters</title> <div sID="gen14826" type="x-p"/> Eze 6:1. <hi type="italic">And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: </hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.2">Eze 6:2</reference> <hi type="italic">. Son of man, turn thy face towards the mountains of Israel, and prophesy against them.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.3">Eze 6:3</reference> <hi type="italic">. And say, Ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord Jehovah: Thus saith the Lord Jehovah to the mountains, and to the hills, to the valleys, and to the low grounds, Behold, I bring the sword upon you, and destroy your high places.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.4">Eze 6:4</reference> <hi type="italic">. Your altars shall be made desolate, and your sun-pillars shall be broken; and I shall make your slain fall in the presence of your idols.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.5">Eze 6:5</reference> <hi type="italic">. And I will lay the corpses of the children of Israel before their idols, and will scatter your bones round about your altars.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.6">Eze 6:6</reference> <hi type="italic">. In all your dwellings shall the cities be made desolate, and the high places waste; that your altars may be desolate and waste, and your idols broken and destroyed, and your sun-pillars hewn down, and the works of your hands exterminated.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.7">Eze 6:7</reference> <hi type="italic">. And the slain will fall in your midst; that you may know that I am Jehovah.</hi> - With <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.1">Eze 6:1</reference> cf. Eze 3:16. The prophet is to prophesy against the mountains of Israel. That the mountains are mentioned (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.2">Eze 6:2</reference>) as <hi type="italic">pars pro toto</hi>, is seen from <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.3">Eze 6:3</reference>, when to the mountains and hills are added also the valleys and low grounds, as the places where idolatry was specially practised; cf. Hos 4:13; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.20">Jer 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.6">Jer 3:6</reference>; see on Hos. <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi> and Deu 12:2. אפיקים, in the older writings, denotes the “river channels,” “the beds of the stream;” but Ezekiel uses the word as equivalent to valley, i.e., נחל, a valley with a brook or stream, like the Arabic wady. גּיא, properly “deepening,” “the deep ground,” “the deep valley;” on the form גּאיות, cf. Ewald, §186 <hi type="italic">da</hi>. The juxtaposition of mountains and hills, of valleys and low grounds, occurs again in <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.4">Eze 36:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.6">Eze 36:6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.35.8">Eze 35:8</reference>; the opposition between mountains and valleys also, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.5-Ezek.32.6">Eze 32:5-6</reference>, and Eze 24:13. The valleys are to be conceived of as furnished with trees and groves, under the shadow of which the worship of Astarte especially was practised; see on v. 15. On the mountains and in the valleys were sanctuaries erected to Baal and Astarte. The announcement of their destruction is appended to the threatening in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference>, which Ezekiel takes up and describes at greater length. Beside the בּמות, the places of sacrifice and worship, and the חמּנים, pillars or statues of Baal, dedicated to him as the sun-god, he names also the altars, which, in Lev. <hi type="italic">l.c. </hi>and other places, are comprehended along with the בּמות eht htiw; see on <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference> and 1Ki 3:3. With the destruction of the idol temples, altars, and statues, the idol-worshippers are also to be smitten, so as to fall down in the presence of their idols. The fundamental meaning of the word גּלּוּלים, “idols,” borrowed from Lev. <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>, and frequently employed by Ezekiel, is uncertain; signifying either “logs of wood,” from גּלל, “to roll” (Gesen.), or <hi type="italic">stercorei</hi>, from גּל, “dung;” not “monuments of stone” (Hävernick). <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.6.5">Eze 6:5</reference></hi> is taken quite literally from <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference></hi>. The ignominy of the destruction is heightened by the bones of the slain idolaters being scattered round about the idol altars. In order that the idolatry may be entirely rooted out, the cities throughout the whole land, and all the high places, are to be devastated, Eze 6:6. The forms תּישׁמנה and יאשׁמוּ are probably not to be derived from שׁמם (Ewald, §138 <hi type="italic">b</hi>), but to be referred back to a stem-form ישׁם, with the signification of שׁמם, the existence of which appears certain from the old name ישׁימון in Ps 68 and elsewhere. The א in יאשׁמו is certainly only <hi type="italic">mater lectonis</hi>. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.7">Eze 6:7</reference>, the singular חלל stands as indefinitely general. The thought, “slain will fall <hi type="italic">in your midst</hi>,” involves the idea that not all the people will fall, but that there will survive some who are saved, and prepares for what follows. The falling of the slain - the idolaters with their idols - leads to the recognition of Jehovah as the omnipotent God, and to conversion to Him.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.8-Ezek.6.10">Eze 6:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen14826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14827" type="x-p"/> The survivors shall go away into banishment amongst the heathen, and shall remember the word of the Lord that will have been fulfilled. - Eze 6:8. <hi type="italic">But I shall preserve a remnant, in that there shall be to you some who have escaped the sword among the nations, when he shall be dispersed among the lands.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.9">Eze 6:9</reference> <hi type="italic">. And those of you who have escaped, will make mention of me among the nations whither they are led captive, when I have broken to me their whorish heart, which had departed from me, and their eyes, which went a whoring after their idols: and they shall loathe themselves because of the evil which they have done in reference to all their abominations.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.10">Eze 6:10</reference> <hi type="italic">. And ye shall know that I am Jehovah. Not in vain have I spoken this evil to you.</hi> - הותיר, <hi type="italic">superstites facere</hi>, “to make or preserve survivors.” The connection with 'בּהיות וגו is analogous to the construction of הותיר, in the sense of “giving a superabundance,” with בּ <hi type="italic">rei</hi>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.11">Deu 28:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.30.9">Deu 30:9</reference>, and is not to be rejected, with Ewald and Hitzig, as inadmissible. For בּהיות is supported by the old versions, and the change of והותרתּי into ודבּרתּי, which would have to be referred to <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.7">Eze 6:7</reference>, is in opposition to the twofold repetition of the וידאתּם כּי אן (וידעוּ), <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.10">Eze 6:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:14</reference>, as this repetition shows that the thought in <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.7">Eze 6:7</reference> is different from that in 17, 21, not “they shall know that Jehovah has spoken,” but “they shall know that He who has done this is Jehovah, the God of Israel.” The preservation of a remnant will be shown in this, that they shall have some who have escaped the sword. הזּרותיכם is <hi type="italic">infin. Niph</hi>. with a plural form of the suffix, as occurs elsewhere only with the plural ending ות of nouns, while Ezekiel has extended it to the ות of the infinitive of ה''ל verbs; cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.31">Eze 16:31</reference>, and Ewald, §259 <hi type="italic">b</hi>. The remembrance of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.9">Eze 6:9</reference>) is the commencement of conversion to Him. אשׁר before נשׁבּרתּי is not to be connected as relative pronoun with לבּם, but is a conjunction, though not used conditionally, “if,” as in <reference osisRef="Lev.4.22">Lev 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.27">Deu 11:27</reference>, and elsewhere, but of time, ὅτε, “when,” as <reference osisRef="Deut.11.6">Deu 11:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.20">2Ch 35:20</reference>, and נשׁבּרתּי in the signification of the <hi type="italic">futur. exact</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> נשׁבּר here is not to be taken as passive, but middle, <hi type="italic">sibi frangere</hi>, i.e., לבּם, <hi type="italic">poenitentiâ conterere animum eorum ut ad ipsum</hi> (<hi type="italic">Deum</hi>) <hi type="italic">redeant</hi> (Maurer, Hävernick). Besides the heart, the eyes also are mentioned, which God is to smite, as the external senses which allure the heart to whoredom. ונקטוּ corresponds to וזכרוּ at the beginning of the verse. קוּט, “the later form for קוּץ, “to feel a loathing,” <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi>, “to be filled with loathing;” cf. <reference osisRef="Job.10.1">Job 10:1</reference> with ב <hi type="italic">object</hi>., “in (on) their פנים, faces,” i.e., their persons or themselves: so also in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.43">Eze 20:43</reference>; Eze 36:31. אל הרעות, in allusion to the evil things; 'לכל־תועב, in reference to all their abominations. This fruit, which is produced by chastisement, namely, that he idolaters are inspired with loathing for themselves, and led to the knowledge of Jehovah, will furnish the proof that God has not spoken in vain.

The remembrance of Jehovah ( Eze 6:9 ) is the commencement of conversion to Him. אשׁר before נשׁבּרתּי is not to be connected as relative pronoun with לבּם, but is a conjunction, though not used conditionally, “if,” as in Lev 4:22 ; Deu 11:27 , and elsewhere, but of time, ὅτε, “when,” as Deu 11:6 and 2Ch 35:20 , and נשׁבּרתּי in the signification of the futur. exact . The Niphal נשׁבּר here is not to be taken as passive, but middle, sibi frangere , i.e., לבּם, poenitentiâ conterere animum eorum ut ad ipsum ( Deum ) redeant (Maurer, Hävernick). Besides the heart, the eyes also are mentioned, which God is to smite, as the external senses which allure the heart to whoredom. ונקטוּ corresponds to וזכרוּ at the beginning of the verse. קוּט, “the later form for קוּץ, “to feel a loathing,” Hiphil , “to be filled with loathing;” cf. Job 10:1 with ב object ., “in (on) their פנים, faces,” i.e., their persons or themselves: so also in Eze 20:43 ; Eze 36:31. אל הרעות, in allusion to the evil things; 'לכל־תועב, in reference to all their abominations. This fruit, which is produced by chastisement, namely, that he idolaters are inspired with loathing for themselves, and led to the knowledge of Jehovah, will furnish the proof that God has not spoken in vain.
